passages.t: The woman on the scarlet beast
passages.happening:
One of the seven angels who had the bowls comes to John: “Come, I will show you the punishment of the great prostitute, who sits on many waters” (verse 1). “The kings of the earth were immoral with her, and those who dwell on the earth were intoxicated with the wine of her immorality” (verse 2).

The angel carries John away in the Spirit into a wilderness, “where I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that was covered with blasphemous names and had seven heads and ten horns” (verse 3).

He describes her: “The woman was dressed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls. She held in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her sexual immorality” (verse 4). “And on her forehead a mysterious name was written: BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF THE ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH” (verse 5).

“I could see that the woman was drunk with the blood of the saints and witnesses for Jesus. And I was utterly amazed at the sight of her” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The seventh bowl ended with God remembering Babylon. Chapters 17 and 18 now slow down and show that judgment closely. Babylon was named in 14:8 and 16:19. Here she is seen for the first time.

The beast she rides is the beast from the sea in chapter 13, the power that demands worship. The woman is the city that rides on it: the glittering culture of wealth, pleasure and pressure that such power makes possible.

The first hearers knew a figure like her. The goddess Roma, the city of Rome pictured as a woman, was worshipped in temples across Asia beside the emperors, and cities such as Pergamum, Smyrna and Ephesus competed for the honour of building them. John takes that proud figure and turns it inside out. The splendid goddess is a prostitute.

That word needs care. The Greek word, pornē, is used here as the prophets used it, of a city or a people that trades faithfulness for gain. Isaiah used it of Tyre for its trade, and Nahum of Nineveh. The charge is not first about private sexual conduct. It is about a whole civilization's seduction: kings and merchants who sell their loyalty for a share of her wealth, and peoples made drunk on what she offers. The figure is a city, not a woman, and nothing in it is a word about women.

Every detail points to that kind of power. Purple and scarlet were the costliest dyes of the ancient world, worn by the rich and powerful. Her golden cup is Jeremiah's picture of Babylon, a golden cup that made the nations drunk. The name on her forehead stands against the seal of God on the foreheads of his servants (7:3; 14:1). And she is ‘drunk with the blood of the saints and witnesses for Jesus’. Her splendour was paid for by the lives of those who would not worship her.

John is ‘utterly amazed’. The vision does not make evil ugly. It makes it attractive, which is why it is dangerous.
passages.ot:
The golden cup is Jeremiah's: “Babylon was a gold cup in the hand of the LORD, making the whole earth drunk. The nations drank her wine; therefore the nations have gone mad” (Jeremiah 51:7). So is the city by the waters: “You who dwell by many waters, rich in treasures, your end has come” (Jeremiah 51:13).

The prophets used the same picture for proud trading cities. Of Tyre, Isaiah wrote that “she will return to hire as a prostitute and sell herself to all the kingdoms on the face of the earth” (Isaiah 23:17). Of Nineveh, Nahum spoke of “the seductive mistress of sorcery, who betrays nations by her prostitution” (Nahum 3:4).
passages.hard:
Who is Babylon?

Christians read Babylon in the four ways the book page sets out, and these notes do not choose. Preterist readers see the prophecy fulfilled largely in the first century: Babylon is Rome, the city that ruled the kings of the earth, or, for some, Jerusalem. Historicist readers, who read Revelation as a chart of the church's history, have often named a church power of their own day as Babylon. Futurist readers expect a final city or world system at the end of history, still to appear. Idealist readers see Babylon as a pattern that comes back in every age: every culture that makes wealth and power into gods and crushes those who refuse them. Many interpreters combine these. The first hearers would have recognized Rome, and the vision also describes something larger than Rome that appears again and again.

This picture has been turned into a weapon more often than almost any other in the Bible. Christians have used it against other Christians: many of the Reformers and those who followed them named a church power of their own day as Babylon, and on the other side commentaries were written partly to answer the Protestant readings of the book. Readers over the centuries have named nations, peoples, leaders and institutions they opposed as Babylon, and every such naming has passed. These notes make no such use of it. They name no nation, city, church, people or movement of our own day as Babylon. The chapter's own call, heard in 18:4, is for God's people to look at their own compromise, not to point at someone else's.

One thing must be said plainly. If the city is Jerusalem, the verse is still no word against the Jewish people. Jesus, his first disciples and the crowds who welcomed him were Jews, and a Roman governor gave the order for his death. For centuries many Christians used scenes like this to justify contempt and violence against Jews. That reading is false. This site rejects it, and the note on Acts 2:22-28 sets out why.

And because the city is pictured as a woman, one more thing must be said. No woman is the target of this picture, and nothing in it gives anyone leave to shame or to harm a woman.
passages.asks: Ask why the vision makes evil look beautiful and admired rather than plainly ugly. Ask where you are tempted to trade loyalty for comfort, standing or gain. And ask whether you read this chapter to find Babylon in someone else, or to find where its cup has reached you.

passages.t: The beast that was, and is not
passages.happening:
The angel asks John, “Why are you so amazed?” and promises, “I will tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast that carries her, which has the seven heads and ten horns” (verse 7).

“The beast that you saw—it was, and now is no more, but is about to come up out of the Abyss and go to its destruction.” And those whose names are not written in the Book of Life “will marvel when they see the beast that was, and is not, and yet will be” (verse 8).

“This calls for a mind with wisdom. The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits. There are also seven kings. Five have fallen, one is, and the other has not yet come; but when he does come, he must remain for only a little while” (verses 9-10). “The beast that was, and now is not, is an eighth king, who belongs to the other seven and is going into destruction” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The chapter has two parts: a vision (verses 1-6) and its explanation (verses 7-18). That is the pattern of Daniel 7, where a heavenly figure explains what the prophet has seen. Even so, the explanation stays symbolic, and it calls for ‘a mind with wisdom’.

The angel promises to tell ‘the mystery’. In the New Testament a mystery is not a puzzle without an answer. It is something hidden that God now makes known: here, what the woman and the beast really are, beneath the splendour.

Listen to the beast's title: it ‘was, and is not, and yet will be’. It is a dark parody of God's own name in 1:4 and 1:8, ‘who is and was and is to come’. The beast copies God's name as it copied the Lamb's death and rising in chapter 13. But its last word is different. God ‘is to come’. The beast is ‘going into destruction’.

‘The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits.’ To a first-century reader that pointed to Rome, famous as the city on seven hills. Roman writers described it that way often, and a coin of the emperor Vespasian, who ruled from AD 69 to 79, shows the goddess Roma seated on seven hills. In the Old Testament mountains can also stand for kingdoms, which fits the next line: the heads are also seven kings.

Then the kings are counted: five fallen, one now, one still to come for a little while, and an eighth who ‘belongs to the other seven’. People have counted them in many ways. Some begin with Julius Caesar, others with Augustus. Some include the three short-lived emperors of AD 68 and 69, Galba, Otho and Vitellius, and some leave them out. On one count the king ‘who is’ is Nero, on another Vespasian, and the count bears on when the book was written. The eighth king, who ‘was, and is not’, has reminded many of the rumour that Nero, who died in AD 68, would return; Roman historians record men who claimed to be him. Other interpreters hold that seven here means what it means everywhere in Revelation, completeness, so the seven kings stand for the whole line of worldly empires rather than a list to be worked out. These notes do not choose.
passages.ot:
The pattern of vision and explanation is Daniel's. Daniel saw a beast that “had ten horns” (Daniel 7:7), and was told what it meant: “And the ten horns are ten kings who will rise from this kingdom” (Daniel 7:24).

Mountains as kingdoms is also Daniel's picture. The stone that struck the statue “became a great mountain and filled the whole earth” (Daniel 2:35), the kingdom of God that “will never be destroyed” (Daniel 2:44).
passages.hard:
Can the seven kings, or the eighth, be named?

For the first century, readers have tried, and the notes above set out their counts; none commands agreement. The four ways of reading take the passage as they take the rest of the book. Preterists count the emperors of Rome and see the first readers' own day. Historicists have matched the heads and kings with powers through the church's history. Futurists often expect the eighth king to be a final ruler still to come. Idealists read the seven as the whole line of empires that demand worship, and the eighth as the pattern coming back again. These notes do not choose.

What these notes will not do is name any king, head or horn as a nation, ruler, office or government of our own day. Confident readings that tied a beast or a horn to a ruler of the reader's own day have come and gone in every generation. The angel calls for ‘a mind with wisdom’. Wisdom here is the power to see what an empire is, beneath its claims, and to refuse it worship.
passages.asks: Ask what it means to you that the beast imitates God's name but cannot finish it. Ask which powers in your world seem to have been here for ever, and what this chapter says about how long they last. And ask whether you are more eager to count the kings than to keep your eyes on the King.

passages.t: Ten kings, and the Lamb who triumphs
passages.happening:
“The ten horns you saw are ten kings who have not yet received a kingdom, but will receive one hour of authority as kings, along with the beast” (verse 12). “These kings have one purpose: to yield their power and authority to the beast” (verse 13).

“They will make war against the Lamb, and the Lamb will triumph over them, because He is Lord of lords and King of kings; and He will be accompanied by His called and chosen and faithful ones” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The ten horns come from Daniel's fourth beast, and the angel says they are ten kings. They have ‘one hour of authority’. In Revelation an hour is a short time. Their power is real, and it is brief.

They have ‘one purpose’: to give their power to the beast. Rulers who could have served justice hand their authority over to the power that demands worship. Then they make war on the Lamb.

And the Lamb wins. The reason given is his name: ‘He is Lord of lords and King of kings’. That title belongs to God in the Old Testament, and here it belongs to the Lamb, the one who conquered by being slain (5:6-9). It will be written on his robe in 19:16. The kings give their power to the beast. The Lamb conquers by giving himself.

His people are with him: ‘called and chosen and faithful’. They do not win the battle. They are with the one who does. Called and chosen are God's work; faithful is how they have lived in response. All three belong together.

Jesus warned that no one can serve God and wealth. This chapter shows what the service of wealth and power becomes when it is built into a whole civilization, and it shows who will have the last word over it.
passages.ot:
The title is the Law's name for God: “For the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great, mighty, and awesome God, showing no partiality and accepting no bribe” (Deuteronomy 10:17). In Revelation the Lamb bears it.

And the kings who join against God and his anointed are Psalm 2's: “The kings of the earth take their stand and the rulers gather together, against the LORD and against His Anointed One” (Psalm 2:2).
passages.hard:
Who are the ten kings?

The text says they have not yet received a kingdom, and will rule for ‘one hour’ with the beast. Readers take them as they take Daniel's ten horns, from which they come. The traditional reading of Daniel saw the ten horns as kings or kingdoms arising from the Roman empire, and many readers of Revelation have followed it. Futurists expect ten kings at the end of the age, joined to a final empire. And because the horn is the Old Testament's standard picture of strength and royal power, others read the ten horns simply as a power with many kings: all the rulers who lend their power to the beast. These notes do not choose.

In many generations readers have matched the ten horns with ten nations, alliances or rulers of their own day, and each match has passed. These notes make none. The chapter's own interest is not in the horns. It is in the Lamb, who triumphs over them.
passages.asks: Ask where you have handed your own ‘authority’, your time, money or loyalty, to a power that does not deserve it. Ask what it means to you that the King of kings conquered by being slain. And ask which of the three words, called, chosen or faithful, you most need to hear today.

passages.t: The beast turns on the city
passages.happening:
The angel goes on: “The waters you saw, where the prostitute was seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and tongues” (verse 15).

“And the ten horns and the beast that you saw will hate the prostitute. They will leave her desolate and naked, and will eat her flesh and burn her with fire” (verse 16). “For God has put it into their hearts to carry out His purpose by uniting to give their kingdom to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled” (verse 17).

“And the woman you saw is the great city that rules over the kings of the earth” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The ‘many waters’ are explained: they are ‘peoples and multitudes and nations and tongues’. The city sits enthroned over the whole world of nations, the same peoples the Lamb bought with his blood (5:9).

Then comes a turn no one expected. The beast and the ten kings turn on the city that rode them. They ‘hate the prostitute’, strip her, devour her and burn her. Evil does not hold together. The power that carried the city ends by destroying it. The picture is of a city laid waste, and it is the beast's violence, not God's people's. It gives no one leave to treat any person this way.

Verse 17 says something stranger still: ‘God has put it into their hearts to carry out His purpose’. The kings think they are serving the beast. In fact God is using even their alliance to bring the city down, ‘until the words of God are fulfilled’. Evil is real and it is violent, but it is never in charge, and in the end it destroys itself.

The last verse names the woman plainly: ‘the great city that rules over the kings of the earth’. For the first hearers that was the city at the centre of their world. Rome sat at the heart of a sea-borne trade that reached from Spain to India. Many early Christians used Babylon as a code name for Rome. Peter's first letter sends greetings from “The church in Babylon” (1 Peter 5:13). Old Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 587 or 586 BC; Rome did the same in AD 70. The name fitted.

Notice too what this chapter sets up. The same words, ‘Come, I will show you’, are spoken in 21:9 by another of the bowl angels, who shows John the bride. The book has two women and two cities: a prostitute and a bride, Babylon and the new Jerusalem, a wilderness and ‘a mountain great and high’ (21:10). One is built on the blood of others. The other is the Lamb's gift.
passages.ot:
The city that seemed to rule for ever is Babylon of the prophets, whose end Jeremiah announced: “You who dwell by many waters, rich in treasures, your end has come; the thread of your life is cut” (Jeremiah 51:13).

And the God who turns the plans of kings to his own purpose is the God of the proverb: “The king’s heart is a waterway in the hand of the LORD; He directs it where He pleases” (Proverbs 21:1).
passages.asks: Ask what it would mean to you to believe that evil, however strong, finally turns on itself. Ask which of the two cities you are being shaped by, and what that looks like in your spending and your loyalties. And ask what it means that God's purpose stands even inside the plans of those who oppose him.
